grammar.title: Grammatik
grammar.rule: kein Brot · keinen Kaffee · keine Milch · nicht kalt · den Tee nicht

tables.caption: keinen Tee · den Tee nicht
rows: Ich kaufe das Brot hier nicht.

grammar.note_en:
Read the noun table left to right as noun, nominative negative, accusative negative. The middle column completes Das ist / Das sind (“That is / Those are”); the last completes Ich finde (“I find”). These example headers identify each role without new German terminology.

Kein negates an indefinite noun or an unspecified amount: Ich finde keinen Tee (“I find no tea / I do not find any tea”), Wir haben kein Brot (“We have no bread”), Wir haben keine Milch (“We have no milk”). It takes the endings already learned with ein/kein: masculine nominative kein, masculine accusative keinen; neuter kein in both; feminine keine; plural keine. The story’s kein Kaffee after ist is a predicate noun in nominative, while keinen Kaffee after findet or trinkt is an accusative object. Follow the noun’s role, not just its position.

Food substances often have no article for an unspecified amount: Wasser (“water”), Milch (“milk”), Brot (“bread”), Butter (“butter”), Käse (“cheese”), Kaffee (“coffee”) and Tee (“tea”). Their negatives use kein rather than adding an indefinite positive article: kein Brot, keine Butter, keinen Käse as an object (“no bread, no butter, no cheese”). Gender still matters even without an article in the positive phrase. A whole loaf can also be ein Brot (“a loaf of bread”), with plural Brote (“loaves”). Ein Ei (“an egg”), Eier (“eggs”) and ein Apfel (“an apple”) are ordinary countable foods. A serving can be ein Kaffee (“a coffee”) even though Kaffee without an article names coffee as a substance. The story shows Emil ordering no particular quantity in Ich trinke Kaffee (“I drink coffee”), then having a serving in Ich trinke einen Kaffee (“I drink a coffee”).

Nicht negates a property or a verb phrase without replacing its noun’s article. Compare Der Kaffee ist nicht kalt (“The coffee is not cold”) and Ich kaufe das Brot hier nicht (“I do not buy the bread here”). The definite object das Brot remains intact. Ich trinke keinen Tee (“I drink no tea / I do not drink tea”) denies an unspecified amount or kind; Ich trinke den Tee nicht (“I do not drink the tea”) rejects the particular tea now in view. In contrastive contexts German can use nicht with a bare noun too; this chapter’s neutral noun negatives use kein. The closed items avoid treating all such possible contrasts as errors: the noun-negative options chiefly test endings, while the nicht gaps negate a property or a phrase with an already specified object.

Do not turn this into a rule that nicht always has one fixed slot. The demonstrated patterns place it before a predicate adjective (nicht kalt) or toward the end after a specified object (den Tee nicht, das Brot hier nicht). The broader clause brackets arrive with later grammar. Noch means “still/yet” here: noch keinen Kaffee (“no coffee yet”) and Das Heft liegt noch im Laden (“The notebook is still in the shop”). Enough is genug: one egg is not enough for six people; the bread and contributed butter are enough for their simpler shared food.

Isst is “eats,” from essen; ich esse is “I eat,” wir essen “we eat” and ihr esst “you [plural] eat.” These actual forms occur in the scene. Trinke, trinkst, trinkt and trinken follow the familiar personal endings for “drink.” Kauft means “buys,” and bezahlt “pays”; choosing and taking a purchase is distinct from handing over the money. Nora brings food she already owns instead of buying it there. The vocabulary cards use finite forms that appear in the prose, without requiring unseen infinitives.

Teuer means “expensive,” billig “cheap”; the reference prices and money stacks make the contrast concrete. They are fictional examples rather than claims about present-day Freiburg prices or the historical currency of the notebook. Warm and kalt mean “warm” and “cold”; steam and the thermometer contrast support the drink-temperature distinction. No adjective ending is required when the adjective follows ist.

The old notebook contains a written price-like sequence beside coffee, tea and bread. No one has established that it sets charges for this new group. Nora points out that contributed butter and the child’s water are missing from it. The closing questions distinguish actual purchases already paid for from an unresolved question about a communal payment rule; they do not settle that rule or the missing-page mystery.
